title: "First half – The claim and its reproduction"

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Slides.** [Open the deck at this half](../../slides/eu-frames-short.html#/first-half-the-claim-and-its-reproduction){target="_blank"} in its own tab, or follow it on the [slides page](slides.qmd).
:::

The first half gives you the vocabulary of three kinds of repetition and the case, a study of how the citizens of the member states frame the European Union, and asks which question its claim answers. Before the break you reproduce the result that one of two independent analysts of the claim recorded, and find out why your number is exactly that number.

## 1. The plan of the session

**On the slides.** The facilitator sets out the two halves and what you do not need: nothing to install, no git, no GitHub or OSF account. Open the browser lab in a tab while the facilitator talks, and leave it to load.

[Open the browser lab](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

## 2. Three kinds of repetition and Multi100

**On the slides.** A matrix of data against analysis separates reproducibility, robustness and replicability. The slides then show Multi100 from the inside: what an analyst received, the two tasks, how the results were put on a common scale, and the five results of this claim, one row at a time.

## 3. Task 1 – The setup check

[Open the browser lab at Task 1](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd#task-1-setup){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

Run the three cells of Task 1 and check that the second reports 270 rows, 27 countries and 10 years. Do it while the slides go on; the lab needs no attention after that.

## 4. The paper and its record

**On the slides.** The Standard Eurobarometer and its question "What does the European Union mean to you personally?", the scales built from the items, the panel of 270 country-years, the model of the original author (OA) and the claim as Multi100 gave it, and what SCORE found when it reproduced and replicated the paper.

## 5. The estimand statement

**On the slides.** The five analysts answered five questions. You write the estimand of the claim in one sentence, hold it, and send it with the rest of the class when the facilitator says go.

## 6. Task 3 – The reproduction

[Open the browser lab at Task 3](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd#task-3-reproduction){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}

Choose one of two analysts and run their cells in order; each cell with gaps to fill has a hint and a full solution under it. Type the analyst and the value, hold them, and send them when the facilitator says go.

| Analyst | Data | Model | Recorded by Multi100 |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| C6HJR | the course panel, 270 country-years | fixed effects for country and year, conventional standard errors | t = −3.804 on 233 df |
| KQXUE | `analyst_KQXUE.csv`, 270 country-years rebuilt from the code of the analyst | a fixed effect for each country, conventional standard errors | t = −7.169 on 242 df |

## 7. Why the numbers differ

**On the slides.** Everyone who chose the same analyst got the same t, and the two analysts did not. The slides set the two fixed-effects models and a model with random intercepts side by side, then show what clustered standard errors and the CR2 test do to the same estimate when twenty-seven countries are the clusters.

**By the end of the half** you have written the estimand statement behind the claim, you have reproduced a recorded result to the third decimal, and you can say why the estimate stays where it is while the test moves.
